topic.name: Triple Integrals in Cylindrical Polar Coordinates

question.text: If the solid region $R$ is given by \[ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \, : \, (x-1)^2 + y^2 \leq 1, \: y \geq 0, \: 1 \leq z \leq 2 \right\}, \] then $\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2+y^2 \: \textrm{d}V =$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(1,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=1,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=2.$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 1$ in polar coordinates:

\begin{align*} (x-1)^2+y^2 &= 1 \\[5pt] (r \cos\theta-1)^2+(r \sin\theta)^2 &= 1 \\[5pt] r^2 \cos^2\theta-2r \cos\theta+1+r^2 \sin^2\theta &= 1 \\[5pt] r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta) -2r\cos\theta &= 0 \\[5pt] r^2 -2r\cos\theta &= 0\\[5pt] r(r-2\cos\theta) &= 0 \end{align*}

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = 2\cos\theta.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2\cos\theta, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 1 \leq z \leq 2 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R x^2+y^2 \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \big( (r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2 \big) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi/2}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2\cos\theta}} \int_{1}^{2} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} r^3 } \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

example.title: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Cylindrical Solid

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 4x \:\textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=4$ for $x\geq 0,$ $y\geq 0$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=y+3.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=y+3 = r\sin\theta +3.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq z \leq r \sin\theta+3 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R 4x \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta 4r\cos{\theta} \cdot r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{r \sin\theta+3} 4r^2\cos{\theta} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2} 4r^2\cos{\theta} \big[ z \big]_{z=0}^{z=r\sin\theta+3} \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2} 4r^2\cos{\theta} (r \sin\theta+3) \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2} 4r^3\cos{\theta}\sin\theta + 12r^2\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2} 2r^3\sin 2\theta + 12r^2\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \left[ \dfrac12r^4\sin 2\theta+ 4r^3\cos\theta \right]_{r=0}^{r=2} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac12 (2)^4\sin 2\theta+ 4(2)^3\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 8\sin 2\theta+ 32\cos\theta \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \big[ -4\cos 2\theta + 32\sin\theta \big]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= -4(-1-1) + 32(1-0)) \\[5pt] &= 40. \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Cylindrical Coordinates

question.text: The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ for $y \leq 0,$ between the surfaces $z = 0$ and $z = x^2 + y^2 + 9.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + 1}} \:\textrm{d}V \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form \[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z = x^2 + y^2 + 9 = r^2 + 9.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: \pi \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq r^2+9\right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + 1}} \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{(r\cos{\theta})^2 + (r\sin{\theta})^2 + 1}} \cdot r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{r^2\cos^2{\theta} + r^2\sin^2{\theta} + 1}} \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{r^2(\cos^2{\theta} + \sin^2{\theta}) + 1}} \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi}}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}r^2+9 }} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{r^2 + 1}}} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}

example.title: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Cylindrical Solid

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2+y^2 \:\textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and between the surfaces $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $z=1.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\sqrt{r^2\cos^2\theta+r^2\sin^2\theta}=r,$ and

  • bounded above by $z=1.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: r \leq z \leq 1 \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R x^2+y^2 \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \left(\left(r\cos\theta\right)^2+\left(r\sin\theta\right)^2\right) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{r}^{1} r^3 \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} r^3 \big[ z \big]_{z=r}^{z=1} \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} r^3 (1-r) \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} r^3- r^4 \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left[ \dfrac{1}{4}r^4 - \dfrac{1}{5}r^5\right]_{r=0}^{r=1} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{5} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{20} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{20}\theta \right]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{20}(2\pi - 0) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{10}. \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Cylindrical Coordinates

question.text: If the solid region $R$ is given by \[ R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \, : \, x^2 + (y+2)^2 \leq 4, \: x \geq 0, \: 0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \right\}, \] then $\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R z(x^2 - y^2) \: \textrm{d}V =$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form \[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \: r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta. \]

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z. \]

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,-2)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

  • bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

  • bounded above by $z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = r.$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x^2 + (y+2)^2 = 4$ in polar coordinates: \begin{align*} x^2 + (y+2)^2 &= 4 \\[5pt] (r\cos{\theta})^2 + (r\sin{\theta} + 2)^2 & = 4 \\[5pt] r^2\cos^2{\theta} + r^2\sin^2{\theta} + 4r\sin{\theta} + 4 & = 4\\[5pt] r^2(\cos^2{\theta} + \sin^2{\theta}) + 4r\sin{\theta} & = 0 \\[5pt] r^2 + 4r\sin{\theta} & = 0\\[5pt] r(r + 4\sin{\theta}) & = 0 \end{align*}

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = -4\sin{\theta}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq -4\sin{\theta}, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq r \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain
\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R z(x^2 - y^2) \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta z\left(\left(r\cos{\theta}\right)^2 - \left(r\sin{\theta}\right)^2 \right) \cdot r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \iiint\limits_\Delta r^3 z \left(\cos^2{\theta} - \sin^2{\theta} \right) \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3\pi/2}}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-4\sin{\theta}}} \int_{0}^{r} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} r^3 z \cos{2\theta} } \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta. \end{align*}
